lessons.title: Knowing your job and your day
lessons.html:
Know what is expected of you

To be organised, you first need to know what your job is. Every worker at a silo or grain farm has tasks: receiving trucks, sampling, cleaning, running conveyors, filling bags, keeping records. Your supervisor should explain your tasks, the standard you must reach and the time you have.

If you are not sure what is expected, ask. Questions to ask your supervisor:

  • What are my main tasks this week?
  • Which task is most important?
  • When must each task be finished?
  • Who do I report to if there is a problem?

Planning your day

Before the shift starts, take five minutes to plan. Write a short list of what you must do today. Put the most important or most urgent tasks at the top.

Type of taskExampleWhen
Urgent and importantTrucks waiting at the intakeNow
Important, not urgentWeekly cleaning of the dust roomPlan a time today
Urgent, not importantPhone call about a meetingQuickly, or pass on
Not urgent, not importantChatting at the gateLater, in your break

Use your time well

During harvest the work is heavy and the days are long. Plan around this. Do preparation work, such as checking tools and cleaning bins, before the trucks start arriving. Keep breaks to the agreed times. If you finish a task early, tell your supervisor and ask what is next.

Be on time

Arriving on time is the first part of being organised. If you will be late or absent, phone your supervisor before the shift starts. Others depend on you: if the sampler is late, the trucks wait and the farmer loses time.

lessons.title: Keeping your work area and records in order
lessons.html:
A place for everything

An organised worker keeps an organised workplace. When tools, forms and PPE are where they should be, you do not waste time looking for them, and fewer accidents happen.

Simple rules for your work area

  • Return every tool to its place after use.
  • Keep walkways and stairs clear of bags, hoses and tools.
  • Label shelves and boxes so that everyone knows what goes where.
  • Throw away rubbish and broken items. Report broken equipment.
  • Keep your PPE clean and stored in your locker or the PPE area.

Records and paperwork

In grain handling, many things must be written down: truck weights, sample results, bin numbers, cleaning checklists and stock counts. Mistakes in records cost money. A wrong bin number can mix grades. A wrong weight can mean a farmer is paid the wrong amount.

Good habits with records:

  1. Write clearly and fill in every space on the form.
  2. Write it down at the time, not at the end of the day from memory.
  3. Check numbers twice.
  4. If you make a mistake, draw one line through it, write the correct value and sign. Do not scratch it out or use correction fluid unless your site rules allow it.
  5. Hand in forms to the right person on time.

Messages and handover

Carry a small notebook. Write down instructions, phone messages and things to report. At the end of the shift, give a short handover to the next person: what is done, what is still open, any problems. This keeps the work flowing across shifts.

Looking after your tools

Check your tools before use. A blunt knife for opening bags or a broken sampling spear slows you down. Report it and get it replaced.

lessons.title: Working with others and growing
lessons.html:
You are part of a team

Being organised also means fitting in with the team. Your work affects other people. If you are slow at the intake, the weighbridge waits. If you do not clean the elevator pit, the next shift starts in a mess.

Communicate clearly

  • Listen carefully to instructions and repeat them back if you are unsure.
  • Tell your supervisor early if you cannot finish a task in time.
  • Ask for help when you need it, and offer help when you can.
  • Speak respectfully, even when you are under pressure.

Handling problems

When something goes wrong, stay calm. Think about what the problem is, what you can do yourself and what you must report. Do not try to fix machines or electrical faults you are not trained for. Report safety problems immediately, for example a missing guard or a slippery floor.

Managing yourself

Being organised includes taking care of yourself. Get enough rest, especially during the harvest season. Drink water and eat during breaks. Tired workers make mistakes and get hurt. Keep personal phone use for break times.

Learning and improving

Think about your own work. What do you do well? What can you do better? Ask your supervisor for feedback. Take part in training. Set yourself a small goal, for example learning to do moisture tests or to operate the forklift once you are trained and authorised. A worker who keeps learning becomes more valuable to the farm and has more chances for promotion.

Key points

  • Know your tasks, the standard and the deadline; ask if you are unsure.
  • Plan your day and do the most important and urgent tasks first.
  • Keep tools, PPE and walkways in order.
  • Write records clearly at the time, check numbers twice and correct mistakes with one line.
  • Communicate early, hand over properly and keep learning.
